title: Dad wants to surprise his son with a Hollow Knight / Mega Man-style platformer starring his favorite character. What's the best AI-assisted stack in 2026?
author: Mobile-Video-8469
selftext:
Hey everyone! I'm a developer (but not a game developer) and I want to surprise my son by building him a small 2D platformer starring his favorite character. Think Mega Man or Hollow Knight vibes: running, jumping, dashing, a few enemies and a boss. Nothing commercial, just a gift from dad.

I lurk here a lot and the one-shot games people post honestly blow my mind. I keep seeing amazing stuff being made with AI coding agents, and games like Astera being built with Blender + Unreal, but I honestly don't know what the right stack is for a *2D* platformer in 2026. My questions:

1. **Engine:** Godot, Unity, GameMaker, or just Phaser/JS in the browser? Which one do AI coding agents (Claude Code, Codex) actually work well with end-to-end?

2. **Art:** what are people using to generate consistent character sprites and animations (idle, run, jump, attack) from a reference image? Any spritesheet tools you'd recommend?

3. **Workflow:** can I realistically get from zero to a playable 2-3 level build in a few weekends by driving an agent, or should I expect to learn the engine properly first?

I'm planning to try this with GPT-6 Astra or Claude Fable as the coding agent. If you've shipped something similar, I'd love to hear what your pipeline looked like. Thanks!

comments.author: TonyDaDesigner
comments.body: you could have just asked an LLM the same question. but.... I like codex, it's great for just about everything. you can have it generate sprite sheets and it will do a great job.  i had my project ported to godot and it's been perfect for my needs.  and yes, you can have this done within a few hours if youre giving it the right prompts. claude is good too but the amount of usage you'll get compared to codex makes it impractical to me. i just built this with codex, took about 6 months but still should give you an idea of whats possible. the only thing I didn't use AI for was the animations:  [https://apps.apple.com/us/app/hood-fight-locked-up/id6798000913](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/hood-fight-locked-up/id6798000913)

replies.author: Fizassist1
replies.body: Godot + codex combo is what I use and love it

replies.author: Quind1
replies.body: By posting here and not just telling him to ask an LLM, other people can learn, too.

comments.author: Mindestiny
comments.body:
If you're going for a one shot, rule Unity out.  

Unity is a *lot* of click ops in the IDE, that's kind of the major selling point - less code, more "logic" for devs who aren't Engineers to better collaborate.  I'm guessing Unreal is much the same as these modern AAA engines were made with heavy focus on empowering the creatives, designers, etc to be more hands on in development without constantly handing everything off to Engineering to write bespoke code for.

replies.author: VyronDaGod
replies.body: Between the mcp and command line, I've been able to have the llm produce good outputs completely headless.

replies.author: Mindestiny
replies.body:
Is that the official Unity connector?

I haven't played around with it yet, every time I've had Claude try to raw dog Unity asset it gets messy because there's a lot of stale temp data/orphaned noise that confuses it.  I wound up building it into my workflows that anything that happens to an asset gets handed off for me to do manually because it just kept making a mess of things.

comments.author: gamedevjp
comments.body: Bevy is a great engine for LLMs as it’s built on Rust. Rust has solid error messages the LLM understands. I use it for game dev and it works great.

comments.author: HyperLightLlama
comments.body:
I'm actually doing something similar! I have been using godot and codex and it's a great combo. As for workflow, I been having some difficulty myself. I have seen that codex is very good at generating concept art, but it has a very tough time translating those concepts into usable sprites at proper dimensions. I have been using pixel lab for animations once I get workable sprites and it's decent, but I've needed to manually edit them to polish for continuity and proper look and feel.
One pitfall that I am currently climbing out of is that if you are designing for a specific device(for me it's my son's retroid pocket classic), make sure you TEST ON THAT DEVICE! I was using godots previews on my desktop to test the levels but when I finally ported it to his retroid, turns out the camera was too zoomed out and everything looked too small for an enjoyable play experience, which has cascaded into a whole bunch of changes and issues. The project is better for it now, but it has been a major setback in my original timeline.
Also don't expect level visual fidelity and quality to match those games right from the start, it's taken a lot of work to make the game look better than a students first flash animation project using MS paint for the assets

replies.author: HyperLightLlama
replies.body: Also, unless you want the agent to spend a huge amount of extra time running validation tests on levels with bots and still create sub par level designs, you should instead have it make tools like decor, stamps, and textures that you can use directly in the editor so you can just make the levels yourself. The llm is really good at helping with things like actual game mechanics like bot behaviors, collision detection, cause and effect interactions(like hitting a switch to unlock a door), so design the level yourself first using the tools it creates for the editor, then it can help you hook everything else up relatively easily

replies.author: BigDealRips
replies.body: This is my pain. Art. I get stun locked.  I think the lesson I’ve learned and one that most people need to do, is sit down and research prompts and how to be effective using them. Keeping things extremely consistent gets the best results.

replies.author: HyperLightLlama
replies.body: Yeah but I think it goes beyond prompt structure and into properly defined skills and workflows that are proven to get the results you want. It's possible, but it's definitely not an area where you can just expect a one shot or for the llm to do most of the heavily lifting right from the beginning
